title: Branches of anthropology: the four fields and applied work
seo_title: Branches of Anthropology: Four Fields Explained Simply
meta_description: The branches of anthropology explained: social and cultural, biological, archaeology, linguistic and applied anthropology, with Indian examples for each.
summary: Anthropology has four classic branches: social or cultural anthropology, which studies living societies; biological or physical anthropology, which studies human evolution and variation; archaeology, which studies past societies through material remains; and linguistic anthropology, which studies language in social life. Applied anthropology puts all four to practical use.

sections.h2: Why anthropology is divided into branches
paras: Anthropology sets out to study humans as a whole: our bodies, our past, our languages and our ways of living together. No single person can master all of that, so the subject is divided into fields. The best known division is the four-field model, associated with Franz Boas in the United States in the early 20th century. It groups the work into social or cultural anthropology, biological or physical anthropology, archaeology and linguistic anthropology.

In India, universities usually teach two main streams, social and cultural anthropology and biological or physical anthropology, with prehistoric archaeology taught inside the anthropology degree. Linguistic anthropology is often handled within social anthropology or by linguistics departments. The fields overlap all the time, and the most interesting research usually sits where two of them meet. If you are new to the subject, start with our guide to [what anthropology is](what-is-anthropology.html).

This is the largest branch. It studies living societies: kinship and marriage, households, economy, politics, law, religion, ritual, art, food and everyday routines. British scholars tended to call it social anthropology, with a focus on social structure and institutions, while American scholars called it cultural anthropology, with a focus on meanings, values and symbols. Today the two labels are used almost interchangeably.

Its core method is [ethnography](what-is-ethnography.html): long-term fieldwork based on participant observation, interviews and careful notes. Indian examples include M. N. Srinivas's work on caste and village life in Karnataka, Irawati Karve's comparative study of kinship across India, and the many studies of tribal communities in central and northeast India. Today social anthropologists in India also work on cities, migration, labour, technology, health and the state.
list: Kinship and family: how relatedness is reckoned, who may marry whom, how property passes on.
Economic anthropology: exchange, markets, gifts, work and livelihood.
Political and legal anthropology: authority, conflict and customary law.
Anthropology of religion: ritual, belief, pilgrimage and sacred places, treated historically and socially.

paras: Biological anthropology studies humans as living organisms. It covers human evolution and the fossil record, primates and their behaviour, human genetics and population history, growth and nutrition, and the ways human bodies vary and adapt to heat, cold, altitude and disease. The older name, physical anthropology, came from a time when the field relied on body measurement. Its early history includes racial classification schemes that are now rejected, and modern biological anthropology stresses that human variation is continuous and does not divide neatly into races.

Specialisations include palaeoanthropology (fossil humans), primatology, human population genetics, forensic anthropology (identifying human remains for legal cases) and bioarchaeology (studying skeletons from archaeological sites). In India, ancient DNA studies of Harappan and later populations have become a lively area. Our [burials and bioarchaeology](burials-and-bioarchaeology.html) session shows how skeletons are read for age, health and diet, and a separate lecture looks at [ancient DNA and the Harappan debate](ancient-dna-and-the-harappan-debate.html) in a neutral, evidence-led way.

sections.h2: Archaeology as a branch of anthropology
paras: Archaeology studies past human life through the things people left behind: tools, pottery, houses, burials, seeds, bones and whole settlements. In the United States it is taught as one of the four fields of anthropology. In India it is taught both inside anthropology departments, usually as prehistoric archaeology, and in separate departments of archaeology and ancient history. The difference is mostly one of emphasis: anthropological archaeology asks broad questions about how societies worked, while history-based archaeology often links finds to texts, dynasties and inscriptions.

Prehistory is where anthropology and archaeology meet most closely. The study of the [Stone Age in India](stone-age-in-india.html), from Acheulian hand axes to the first farming villages, depends on both stone tool analysis and comparison with living hunter-gatherers. A good way to see this in practice is a hands-on [stone tools session](stone-tools-up-close.html), where students handle replicas and learn how tools were made and classified.

Linguistic anthropology studies language as part of social life. It asks how people use speech to show respect, claim identity, tell stories, argue and pray, and how language connects to thought and to power. It overlaps with sociolinguistics and with the documentation of endangered languages.

India is an obvious place for this work. The country has languages from several families, including Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman, and many people switch between two or three languages in a single day. Linguistic anthropologists in India record oral traditions, study multilingual households and markets, and help communities document languages that are spoken by small numbers of people. Folklore and oral history are natural meeting points with this branch.

sections.h2: Applied anthropology: putting the fields to work
paras: Applied anthropology uses the methods and knowledge of all four fields to solve practical problems. It is sometimes counted as a fifth branch and sometimes as a dimension that runs through the other four. Applied anthropologists work in public health, development projects, education, environmental planning, disaster relief, museums, heritage management, forensic identification and user research for companies.

In India, anthropologists have contributed to resettlement and rehabilitation studies, forest rights work, tribal welfare planning, public health campaigns and museum interpretation. The ethical questions are serious: who asked for the research, who benefits from it, and whether the community agreed to it. Good applied work starts by listening. Practical training in this listening, such as an [oral history and neighbourhood memory lab](oral-history-and-neighbourhood-memory-lab.html), is a useful first step for students who want to do applied work later.

If you enjoy people, conversation and writing, social and cultural anthropology is the natural fit. If you prefer laboratory work, biology and statistics, choose biological anthropology. If you like fieldwork outdoors and objects, archaeology suits you. If languages fascinate you, look at linguistic anthropology or linguistics. Most degree courses in India expose you to all of them in the first year, so you can decide once you have tried each.

Museums are a good way to see the branches side by side. A visit to the [Bhopal Tribal Museum](bhopal-tribal-museum-material-culture-interpretation.html) brings together material culture, ritual, art and language from the communities of Madhya Pradesh, and makes the links between the fields easy to see. Students preparing for the civil services will find that the anthropology optional for UPSC covers all four branches, with a strong focus on India.

faq.q: What are the four branches of anthropology?
faq.a: The four classic branches are social or cultural anthropology, biological or physical anthropology, archaeology, and linguistic anthropology. This four-field model is linked with Franz Boas and is still used in many universities. Applied anthropology is often added as a fifth branch or treated as a practical side of all four.

faq.q: What is the difference between social and cultural anthropology?
faq.a: The difference is mostly historical. British anthropologists used the term social anthropology and focused on social structure and institutions such as kinship and politics. American anthropologists used cultural anthropology and focused on meanings, symbols and values. Today most departments treat them as one field with two emphases.

faq.q: Is physical anthropology the same as biological anthropology?
faq.a: Yes. Physical anthropology is the older name, from when the field relied mainly on measuring bodies and skeletons. Biological anthropology is the modern name and reflects the wider use of genetics, ecology, nutrition and evolutionary biology. Many Indian universities still use the older name for courses and departments.

faq.q: Which branch of anthropology is best for a career?
faq.a: It depends on your interests. Social anthropology leads to research, development work, policy, user research and teaching. Biological anthropology leads to forensic work, genetics and public health research. Archaeology leads to excavation, museums and heritage work. Linguistic anthropology suits language documentation and education.

faq.q: Is archaeology part of anthropology in India?
faq.a: Partly. Anthropology departments in India usually teach prehistoric archaeology as part of the degree. Separate departments of archaeology, or of ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology, teach the subject with a stronger link to history, texts and inscriptions. Both routes can lead to fieldwork and research careers.

posts.hook: Anthropology has four branches, and one of them is archaeology.
posts.caption: Social, biological, archaeological and linguistic anthropology all ask how humans live and how we came to live this way. In India, prehistory is usually taught inside the anthropology degree. Our new guide explains each branch with Indian examples.

posts.hook: See all four branches in one museum visit.
posts.caption: At a good ethnographic museum, look at the tools (archaeology), the textiles and ritual objects (cultural), the labels in local languages (linguistic) and any displays on food and health (biological). The links appear quickly.

posts.hook: Let your class try anthropology with their hands.
posts.caption: We run stone tools sessions, a bioarchaeology lecture and an oral history lab for schools and colleges. Each one works online or on your campus, anywhere in India.
